While party leaders have pledged swift action on healthcare and household costs, turning that agenda into law will run straight into Trump’s veto pen. This morning, we look at what a Democratic-controlled Congress changes —and what it doesn’t.

   • Stock futures rebounded as investors weighed the Democrats’ election sweep.

   • Hackers are cranking the heat on Europe’s supermarket freezers to above 120 degrees.

   • North Korea accelerated a spree of missile tests, signaling it would stick to its guns as it spurned U.S. diplomatic overtures with a growing list of demands.

   • Pieces of the tail of the Bahamas-bound business jet that crashed in Florida have been found miles away from the impact site, indicating that part of the aircraft separated before the plane hit the ground.

   • 3M has agreed to pay $7.35 billion over nine years to people who have made personal-injury claims related to firefighting foam that contained so-called forever chemicals known as PFAS.

On Tuesday, third-quarter results that weren’t quite rosy enough sent the stock down by almost 9%. Get Spencer’s Markets A.M. newsletter in your inbox . 

   • CVS Health will split into two companies , dividing its retail pharmacies from its insurance and pharmacy-benefit operations in a move that will reverse one of its signature deals.

   • The canned-cocktail trend that liquor companies steered clear of in recent years isn’t going away and they are scrambling to catch up, writes Carol Ryan.

READ IT HERE FIRST   Iran turns to guerrilla tactics to reassert its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.   Tehran is using everything in its arsenal to try to disrupt the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf as it tries to shore up the regime’s fast-eroding position in the conflict and pressure the Trump administration in deadlocked negotiations. Over recent weeks, Tehran has launched bomb-laden undersea drones, fired rocket-propelled grenades and deployed crews to attach limpet mines to ships, targeting vessels that shuttle oil to waiting tankers, report Summer Said, Benoit Faucon and Georgi Kantchev. The Islamic Republic’s battle to block that escape route has become a shadow war inside the wider U.S.-Iran conflict, with a direct impact on global energy prices as American forces have struck back.

   5.   Silicon Valley promises AI will cure disease. Drugmaker CEOs aren’t buying it.   Anthropic’s chief executive said AI could cure most human diseases within a decade. Another tech exec joked that AI researchers have started smoking cigarettes because they are so confident AI will cure lung cancer. Drugmakers are certainly using AI—even to come up with new drugs. Yet in the race to integrate AI into medicine, a sharp divide has emerged between Silicon Valley’s promises and what pharma execs say are the harsh realities of drugmaking, reports Xavier Martinez. There are still many unknowns with biology that data analysis can’t fix.

On a recent night just past 2 a.m., the field biologist scooped up a wire trap containing a furious, hissing carnivore—part of an urgent mission across the Great Plains to save the black-footed ferret from extinction . Drought, plague and dwindling numbers of prairie dogs, ferrets’ main food source, have battered the population. For C-suiters conscious of bottom lines, the seating behind Celebrity Row is often a steal. Those comparatively lower prices are a reason why purchases of second-row Knicks seats on StubHub are roughly three times as high as sales of those courtside.

DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ   It’s hard to imagine a more rabid fan base than Hallmark holiday movie devotees. To see what happens when you put thousands of them on a ship together, our travel columnist Dawn Gilbertson went on the annual Hallmark Christmas Cruise . A sold-out, four-night extravaganza, it is a passion project that begins long before the suitcases come out with holiday merch, the tackier the better. One cruiser put it perfectly: “It’s almost like summer camp for people that love Christmas movies.”

Democrats Take Congress as Trump Says Iran War Is Partly to Blame for GOP Losses
 
Plus, Iran turns to guerrilla tactics to try to stop the flow of oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz, and CVS Health decides to split in two
 
 
JABIN BOTSFORD FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Two years after handing Republicans control of Washington, voters flipped Congress blue, resetting the balance of power for President Trump’s final years in office.

 

The sweep gives Democrats decisive leverage over everything from Trump’s nominees to government spending. While party leaders have pledged swift action on healthcare and household costs, turning that agenda into law will run straight into Trump’s veto pen. This morning, we look at what a Democratic-controlled Congress changes—and what it doesn’t.

 

Got questions about the results? Washington Coverage Chief Damian Paletta will be available for a real-time written chat from 2-3 p.m. ET today. Submit your questions at any time here.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Trump said the conflict in Iran was partially to blame for widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections. In an interview with the Journal on Tuesday night, he maintained that he didn’t regret launching the war.

 

• Stock futures rebounded as investors weighed the Democrats’ election sweep.

 

• Hackers are cranking the heat on Europe’s supermarket freezers to above 120 degrees.

 

• North Korea accelerated a spree of missile tests, signaling it would stick to its guns as it spurned U.S. diplomatic overtures with a growing list of demands.

 

• Pieces of the tail of the Bahamas-bound business jet that crashed in Florida have been found miles away from the impact site, indicating that part of the aircraft separated before the plane hit the ground.

 

• 3M has agreed to pay $7.35 billion over nine years to people who have made personal-injury claims related to firefighting foam that contained so-called forever chemicals known as PFAS.

• CVS Health will split into two companies, dividing its retail pharmacies from its insurance and pharmacy-benefit operations in a move that will reverse one of its signature deals.

 

• The canned-cocktail trend that liquor companies steered clear of in recent years isn’t going away and they are scrambling to catch up, writes Carol Ryan.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Iran turns to guerrilla tactics to reassert its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.

 

Tehran is using everything in its arsenal to try to disrupt the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf as it tries to shore up the regime’s fast-eroding position in the conflict and pressure the Trump administration in deadlocked negotiations. Over recent weeks, Tehran has launched bomb-laden undersea drones, fired rocket-propelled grenades and deployed crews to attach limpet mines to ships, targeting vessels that shuttle oil to waiting tankers, report Summer Said, Benoit Faucon and Georgi Kantchev. The Islamic Republic’s battle to block that escape route has become a shadow war inside the wider U.S.-Iran conflict, with a direct impact on global energy prices as American forces have struck back.

 

5.

 

Silicon Valley promises AI will cure disease. Drugmaker CEOs aren’t buying it.

 

Anthropic’s chief executive said AI could cure most human diseases within a decade. Another tech exec joked that AI researchers have started smoking cigarettes because they are so confident AI will cure lung cancer. Drugmakers are certainly using AI—even to come up with new drugs. Yet in the race to integrate AI into medicine, a sharp divide has emerged between Silicon Valley’s promises and what pharma execs say are the harsh realities of drugmaking, reports Xavier Martinez. There are still many unknowns with biology that data analysis can’t fix.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Biologists are pulling graveyard shifts to save America’s rarest predator.

 
 
A black-footed ferret. TRAVIS LIVIERI
 

To the nocturnal creatures of South Dakota’s prairie, Travis Livieri fancies himself an alien abductor. On a recent night just past 2 a.m., the field biologist scooped up a wire trap containing a furious, hissing carnivore—part of an urgent mission across the Great Plains to save the black-footed ferret from extinction. Drought, plague and dwindling numbers of prairie dogs, ferrets’ main food source, have battered the population. Amira McKee spent a night out with the biologists racing to pull America’s rarest predator back from the brink.

• Economic Data: ADP releases its October private-sector employment report, and the ISM releases its services index. 

 

• Earnings: Uber, McDonald’s, Kraft Heinz, DoorDash, Snap, Qualcomm, CVS Health, Novo Nordisk

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
$7,100
 

The rough price of seats right behind courtside for the New York Knicks’ home opener on SeatGeek. For C-suiters conscious of bottom lines, the seating behind Celebrity Row is often a steal. Those comparatively lower prices are a reason why purchases of second-row Knicks seats on StubHub are roughly three times as high as sales of those courtside.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Our columnist went on a Hallmark cruise with fans who can’t get enough of Christmas.

 
 
Hallmark movie superfans line up to board the 2026 Hallmark Christmas Cruise in Miami. DAWN GILBERTSON/WSJ
 

It’s hard to imagine a more rabid fan base than Hallmark holiday movie devotees. To see what happens when you put thousands of them on a ship together, our travel columnist Dawn Gilbertson went on the annual Hallmark Christmas Cruise. A sold-out, four-night extravaganza, it is a passion project that begins long before the suitcases come out with holiday merch, the tackier the better. One cruiser put it perfectly: “It’s almost like summer camp for people that love Christmas movies.”
